classification.difficultyReason: Find linear factors, divide to reduce the polynomial degree, and apply the zero-product property to cubic and quartic equations.

answer.worked:
Let $P(x)=2x^3+5x^2-x-6$.
$$\begin{align*}P(1)&=2+5-1-6\\P(1)&=0\end{align*}$$
Thus $x-1$ is a factor. Long division gives:
$$\begin{array}{r}2x^2+7x+6\\\hline\end{array}$$
The successive subtractions are:
$$\begin{align*}P(x)-2x^2(x-1)&=7x^2-x-6\\(7x^2-x-6)-7x(x-1)&=6x-6\\(6x-6)-6(x-1)&=0\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$\begin{align*}P(x)&=(x-1)(2x^2+7x+6)\\P(x)&=(x-1)(x+2)(2x+3)\end{align*}$$
By the zero-product property, $x=1$, $x=-2$ or $x=-\frac32$.

Let $P(x)=2x^4-x^3-8x^2+x+6$.
$$\begin{align*}P(1)&=2-1-8+1+6\\P(1)&=0\end{align*}$$
Thus $x-1$ is a factor. In long division, the successive subtractions are:
$$\begin{align*}P(x)-2x^3(x-1)&=x^3-8x^2+x+6\\(x^3-8x^2+x+6)-x^2(x-1)&=-7x^2+x+6\\(-7x^2+x+6)+7x(x-1)&=-6x+6\\(-6x+6)+6(x-1)&=0\end{align*}$$
Therefore $P(x)=(x-1)Q(x)$, where $Q(x)=2x^3+x^2-7x-6$.
$$\begin{align*}Q(2)&=16+4-14-6\\Q(2)&=0\end{align*}$$
Thus $x-2$ is a factor of $Q(x)$. A second long division gives:
$$\begin{align*}Q(x)-2x^2(x-2)&=5x^2-7x-6\\(5x^2-7x-6)-5x(x-2)&=3x-6\\(3x-6)-3(x-2)&=0\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$\begin{align*}P(x)&=(x-1)(x-2)(2x^2+5x+3)\\P(x)&=(x-1)(x-2)(x+1)(2x+3)\end{align*}$$
By the zero-product property, $x=1$, $x=2$, $x=-1$ or $x=-\frac32$.
